How war-risk pricing works

When a merchant vessel transits an area that marine underwriters consider risky, the standard hull policy is not enough. Shipowners buy war-risk cover — an additional premium, usually quoted as a percentage of the vessel's insured value, for a defined period, often in 7-day blocks. Areas are listed by market bodies when perceived risk rises, and entering a listed area without the required cover can void the policy.

The price moves with perceived risk: regional tension, incident reports, naval activity and reinsurance costs all feed into underwriters' assessments. A higher premium does not just affect the shipowner — it is passed through the charter chain and ultimately raises the delivered cost of crude oil, LNG and containerised goods for importers and consumers.

Alongside hull war-risk cover, owners arrange related products: P&I clubs provide mutual liability cover, loss-of-hire insurance protects earnings lost during delays, and charterers may take contingency cover of their own. Together these products form the insurance cost of a transit — a cost that spikes far faster than freight rates when tensions rise.
